issues.title: 01_chemistry_hamiltonian tutorial energy plot scale
issues.body:
The scale in the energy plot in the [chemistry tutorial](https://github.com/Qiskit/qiskit-addon-sqd/blob/stable/0.6/docs/tutorials/01_chemistry_hamiltonian.ipynb) is a little misleading. For a non-chemist, with little to no knowledge of the energies required for chemical accuracy, the way the results are plotted makes it look like the energy has basically converged to the exact value. This would be problematic because the tutorial uses bitstrings sampled from a uniform distribution and apparently returns an answer close to exact, thus implying that running on a real backend is not necessary.
From discussion with @kevinsung the energy difference of the converged result with the exact is actually very far from chemical accuracy. So uniform sampling is actually not giving such a great result. 

### Any suggestions?

One possibility is plot the results at a different scale. For example, plotting the exact solution with a shaded area around it to indicate chemical accuracy together with the solution obtained with SQD on random samples could highlight how far the obtained solution is from the right answer

issues.title: Users can't map wavefunc coeffs to the corresponding configuration
issues.body:
### Environment

All environments

### What is happening and why is it wrong?

The wavefunction coefficients returned from `solve_fermion` are stored in an ``MxN`` matrix, where ``M`` is the number of unique alpha determinants and ``N`` is the number of unique beta determinants. The rows and columns are associated with the sorted (ascending) determinants.

Since users pass in a bitstring matrix, they have no way of knowing to what configuration each amplitude is associated (Keep in mind the output configurations don't even have to be present in the set of input configurations.)

### Any suggestions?

The user should be returned a mapping from configuration to amplitude. The most straightforward thing to do would be to return a ``dict[int, float]`` mapping the full spin configuration to the associated amplitude.

We could also return a tuple as shown [here](https://github.com/qiskit-community/ffsim/blob/f40e524bd11fda8b64ae7c7670a7c4e187e41e92/python/ffsim/molecular_data.py#L241).

issues.title: Orbital optimization uses redundant parameters
issues.body:
The orbital optimization routine accepts a list of parameters `k_flat` of length `n_orbitals**2`. It is then used to construct an antisymmetric matrix: https://github.com/Qiskit/qiskit-addon-sqd/blob/9b57485a8461ef45b98fa064d1f83018aebb9490/qiskit_addon_sqd/fermion.py#L523-L524

A real-valued antisymmetric matrix is parameterized by its upper triangle excluding the diagonal, so only `n_orbitals * (n_orbitals - 1) / 2` parameters are needed. Eliminating the redundant parameters should improve the convergence of the optimization.

issues.title: Function to create singles and doubles transitions.
issues.body:
### What should we add?

It would be useful to give users functions to create singles and doubles transitions instead of asking them to code it themselves like in [this](https://qiskit.github.io/qiskit-addon-sqd/how_tos/add_fermionic_excitations_to_configuration_pool.html) tutorial.

Supposing one has the code to calculate the transitions it could work something like this:

```
import numpy as np
from qiskit_addon_sqd.fermion import create_transitions_doubles_within_same_spin, create_transitions_doubles_across_spin, create_transitions_single

transitions_single = create_transitions_single(norb)
transitions_doubles_same = create_transitions_doubles_within_same_spin(norb)
transitions_doubles_across= ccreate_transitions_doubles_across_spin(norb)
    
# Create the identity transition
identity_transition = np.array([['I'] * (2 * norb)], dtype='<U1')
    
# Combine all transitions
transitions_combined = np.vstack([transitions_single, transitions_doubles_same,transitions_doubles_across, identity_transition])
```

Then a user could easily create whichever transitions it wanted and include then with `enlarge_batch_from_transitions`.

I could work on this if people think it would be useful.

issues.title: Add Support for Adaptive Sample Selection in Sample-Based Quantum Diagonalization (SQD)
issues.body:
### What should we add?

I would like to request the addition of adaptive sample selection capabilities to the Qiskit addon for sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD). Adaptive sampling would enhance the efficiency and robustness of SQD by dynamically selecting the most informative samples during the iterative diagonalization process.

Motivation:
Improved Efficiency:

Current SQD implementations rely on user-provided samples obtained through predefined quantum circuits. While effective, this static approach might require a large number of samples for convergence, especially for challenging systems.
Adaptive sample selection can reduce the required sample size by focusing computational resources on sampling regions that contribute the most to the subspace expansion.
Enhanced Robustness:

Quantum noise can corrupt samples, impacting the accuracy of the diagonalization process. Adaptive sampling techniques could prioritize high-fidelity samples or refine the representation of subspaces impacted by noise.
Targeting Sparse Eigenstates:

The convergence rate of SQD improves with the sparseness of the target eigenstate. Adaptive sampling could dynamically identify and enhance contributions from relevant subspaces, further accelerating convergence.

Adaptive sampling is increasingly used in hybrid quantum-classical algorithms (e.g., Variational Quantum Eigensolvers). Adding it to SQD would align the tool with modern practices in quantum computing.
Proposed Implementation:
Dynamic Sample Evaluation:

Implement a mechanism to evaluate the quality or contribution of each sample to the subspace expansion. Metrics could include fidelity, overlap with existing subspace vectors, or contributions to the Hamiltonian's representation.
Feedback Loop:

Add a feedback loop between the classical solver and the quantum sampler to iteratively refine the sampling process.
Heuristics for Sample Prioritization:

Develop heuristics to identify underrepresented subspaces or improve sample diversity. For instance, sampling could focus on regions where the subspace projection has the highest residual errors.

References
https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.07417
https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-63778-0_23

issues.title: Refine type hint for `solve_fermion()`'s 'spin_sq` argument
issues.body: In [solve_fermion()](https://github.com/Qiskit/qiskit-addon-sqd/blob/main/qiskit_addon_sqd/fermion.py#L79), the type hint for `spin_sq` parameter should be `float` instead of `int`. This parameter represents spin squared expectation value of the target ground state `S^2 = s(s+1)`, where `s` is the spin quantum number taking values of $\frac{n}{2}$ (n being an integer). Therefore, `spin_sq` should accept float values.

issues.title: solve_fermion returns incorrect energy when spin is contaminated
issues.body:
### What should we add?

PySCF is not guaranteed to return a wavefunction with the requested spin squared. When the spin squared deviates from the value requested, then `e_sci` in this line is not the energy of the wavefunction.
https://github.com/Qiskit/qiskit-addon-sqd/blob/6a882f6407768a8eae0d5f6c1bf851b4aa875514/qiskit_addon_sqd/fermion.py#L135

Mario investigated and found this to be apparently the correct formula:
```
e_sci = e_sci-myci.ss_penalty*(spin_sq-spin_squared)**2
```

But there may be situations where it is not correct. In PySCF's normal FCI class, there is an `e_tot` attribute which is supposed to always return the energy, but SelectedCI doesn't have that. The surest thing to do is just to compute the energy directly from the RDMs:
```python
dm1 = myci.make_rdm1(sci_vec, norb, (num_up, num_dn))
dm2 = myci.make_rdm2(sci_vec, norb, (num_up, num_dn))
e_sci = np.einsum('pr,pr->',dm1,hcore)+0.5*np.einsum('prqs,prqs->',dm2,eri)
```
(courtesy of Mario)

issues.title: SQD seems to sometimes produce non-variational energies for fermionic systems.
issues.body:
### Environment

- **qiskit-addon-sqd version**:  0.9.0 and 0.8.0
- **Python version**:  3.12
- **Operating system**: Fedora 41

(Also using Qiskit 1.2.2, qiskit-aer 0.15.0, qiskit algorithms 0.3.0, qiskit-ibm-runtime 0.33.2, and qiskit-nature 0.7.2.)

### What is happening and why is it wrong?

Running SQD seems to sometimes (not always) produce ground state energies that are unphysical in that they are lower than the exact FCI ground state energy. I am unsure if this is an actual bug or user error on my part. If it is the latter, any insight as to what I am doing wrong would be greatly appreciated.

### How can we reproduce the issue?

This code closely follows the nitrogen dimer example in the documentation, but with some key differences:

1. It uses a different molecule, H2.
2. It is using `AerSimulator` as the backend instead of `FakeSherbrooke`.
3. It is using PySCF's `FCI` functionality instead of `CASCI`. 

When I run this code, it produces either -2.31 (not variational) or -1.47 (bad accuracy) for the electronic energy when the exact FCI energy is -1.857 Hartree.

```
import warnings

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

from pyscf import ao2mo, cc, gto, scf, cc, fci
import ffsim
import numpy as np

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit, QuantumRegister
from qiskit.transpiler.preset_passmanagers import generate_preset_pass_manager
from qiskit_ibm_runtime import SamplerV2 as Sampler, SamplerOptions
from qiskit_aer.aerprovider import AerSimulator

from qiskit_addon_sqd.counts import counts_to_arrays
from qiskit_addon_sqd.configuration_recovery import recover_configurations
from qiskit_addon_sqd.fermion import (
    flip_orbital_occupancies,
    solve_fermion,
)
from qiskit_addon_sqd.subsampling import postselect_and_subsample

basis = "sto-3g"
interatomic_distance = 0.735

mol_h2 = gto.M(atom=f'H 0 0 0; H 0 0 {interatomic_distance}', basis=basis)
mf_h2 = scf.RHF(mol=mol_h2)
mf_h2.run()
mf_h2.kernel()
num_spin_orbitals = int(2*mol_h2.nao)
num_spatial_orbitals = int(mol_h2.nao)
nuclear_repulsion_energy = mf_h2.mol.energy_nuc()
num_electrons = mol_h2.nelectron
nelec = (int(num_electrons // 2), int(num_electrons // 2))
num_alpha = nelec[0]
num_beta = nelec[1]

hcore = mf_h2.get_hcore()
eri = mf_h2._eri
eri = ao2mo.restore(1, eri, num_spatial_orbitals)
mf_h2.kernel()
hchain_cc = cc.CCSD(mf_h2)
hchain_cc.kernel()
t1 = hchain_cc.t1
t2 = hchain_cc.t2

cisolver = fci.FCI(mf_h2, mf_h2.mo_coeff).run(nroots=4)
cisolver.kernel()
print(f'E(FCI) = {cisolver.kernel()[0]}')

seed = 111
nshots = 10**3
sampler = Sampler(mode=AerSimulator(), options=SamplerOptions(default_shots=nshots))

solver_kwargs = {"spin_sq": 0,
                 "open_shell": False,
                 "configuration_recovery_iterations": 10,
                 "num_batches": 100,
                 "samples_per_batch": 10**3,
                 "max_davidson_cycles": 10**3,
                 "seed": 111,
                 "sampler": sampler}

iterations = solver_kwargs["configuration_recovery_iterations"]
n_batches = solver_kwargs["num_batches"]
open_shell = solver_kwargs["open_shell"]
samples_per_batch = solver_kwargs["samples_per_batch"]
seed = solver_kwargs["seed"]
sampler = solver_kwargs["sampler"]
max_davidson_cycles = solver_kwargs["max_davidson_cycles"]
spin_sq = solver_kwargs["spin_sq"]

alpha_alpha_indices = [(p, p + 1) for p in range(num_spatial_orbitals - 1)]
alpha_beta_indices = [(p, p) for p in range(0, num_spatial_orbitals, 4)]

ansatz_kwargs = {"n_reps": 1,
                 "t1": t1,
                 "t2": t2,
                 "interaction_pairs": (alpha_alpha_indices, alpha_beta_indices)}

ucj_op = ffsim.UCJOpSpinBalanced.from_t_amplitudes(**ansatz_kwargs)

qubits = QuantumRegister(2 * num_spatial_orbitals, name="q")
circuit = QuantumCircuit(qubits)

circuit.append(ffsim.qiskit.PrepareHartreeFockJW(num_spatial_orbitals, nelec), qubits)

circuit.append(ffsim.qiskit.UCJOpSpinBalancedJW(ucj_op), qubits)
circuit.measure_all()

pass_manager = generate_preset_pass_manager(optimization_level=3,
                                            backend=sampler.backend(),
                                            initial_layout=None)

isa_circuit = pass_manager.run(circuit)
pass_manager.pre_init = ffsim.qiskit.PRE_INIT
isa_circuit = pass_manager.run(circuit)
job = sampler.run([isa_circuit])

counts = job.result()[0].data.meas.get_counts()
bitstring_matrix_full, probs_arr_full = counts_to_arrays(counts)

occupancies_bitwise = None
for i in range(iterations):

    if occupancies_bitwise is None:
        bs_mat_tmp = bitstring_matrix_full
        probs_arr_tmp = probs_arr_full

    else:
        bs_mat_tmp, probs_arr_tmp = recover_configurations(
            bitstring_matrix_full,
            probs_arr_full,
            occupancies_bitwise,
            num_alpha,
            num_beta,
            rand_seed=seed,
            )
        
batches = postselect_and_subsample(
bs_mat_tmp,
probs_arr_tmp,
hamming_right=num_alpha,
hamming_left=num_beta,
samples_per_batch=solver_kwargs["samples_per_batch"],
num_batches=solver_kwargs["num_batches"],
rand_seed=solver_kwargs["seed"],
)

pass_manager = generate_preset_pass_manager(optimization_level=3,
                                            backend=sampler.backend(),
                                            initial_layout=None)

circuit.measure_all()
isa_circuit = pass_manager.run(circuit)
pass_manager.pre_init = ffsim.qiskit.PRE_INIT
isa_circuit = pass_manager.run(circuit)
job = sampler.run([isa_circuit])
counts = job.result()[0].data.meas.get_counts()
bitstring_matrix_full, probs_arr_full = counts_to_arrays(counts)

occupancies_bitwise = None

e_hist = np.zeros((iterations, n_batches))  # energy history
s_hist = np.zeros((iterations, n_batches))  # spin history
occupancy_hist = np.zeros((iterations, 2 * num_spatial_orbitals))

for i in range(iterations):

    if occupancies_bitwise is None:
        bs_mat_tmp = bitstring_matrix_full
        probs_arr_tmp = probs_arr_full

    else:
        bs_mat_tmp, probs_arr_tmp = recover_configurations(
            bitstring_matrix_full,
            probs_arr_full,
            occupancies_bitwise,
            num_alpha,
            num_beta,
            rand_seed=seed,
            )
        
    batches = postselect_and_subsample(
    bs_mat_tmp,
    probs_arr_tmp,
    hamming_right=num_alpha,
    hamming_left=num_beta,
    samples_per_batch=samples_per_batch,
    num_batches=n_batches,
    rand_seed=seed,
    )

    e_tmp = np.zeros(n_batches)
    s_tmp = np.zeros(n_batches)
    occs_tmp = np.zeros((n_batches, 2 * num_spatial_orbitals))
    coeffs = []
    eigval_eigvec_pairs = {}
    for j in range(n_batches):
        energy_sci, coeffs_sci, avg_occs, spin = solve_fermion(
            batches[j],
            hcore,
            eri,
            open_shell=open_shell,
            spin_sq=spin_sq,
            max_davidson=max_davidson_cycles,
        )
        e_tmp[j] = energy_sci
        s_tmp[j] = spin
        occs_tmp[j, :num_spatial_orbitals] = avg_occs[0]
        occs_tmp[j, num_spatial_orbitals:] = avg_occs[1]
        coeffs.append(coeffs_sci)

        eigval_eigvec_pairs[energy_sci] = coeffs_sci

    avg_occupancy = np.mean(occs_tmp, axis=0)
    occupancies_bitwise = flip_orbital_occupancies(avg_occupancy)

    e_hist[i, :] = e_tmp
    s_hist[i, :] = s_tmp
    occupancy_hist[i, :] = avg_occupancy

minimum_energy = min(e_tmp)
minimum_eigenvector = eigval_eigvec_pairs[min(e_tmp)]

exact_energy = cisolver.kernel()[0] - nuclear_repulsion_energy
e_diff = [abs(np.min(energies) - exact_energy) for energies in e_hist]

sqd_energy = min([np.min(energies) for energies in e_hist])

print(f'FCI electronic energies: {cisolver.kernel()[0] - nuclear_repulsion_energy}')
print(f'SQD energy: {sqd_energy}')

```

### Traceback

_No response_

### Any suggestions?

It could be related to #140 , I am not sure. The non-variational nature of the result seems to suggest it has something to do with either the values of `hcore` and `eri` that are being passed to `solve_fermion` or how `solve_fermion` is processing them in certain cases. i.e. even if the issue was with another variable such as the particle number, spin sector, the subspace in which the selected CI step is being performed, the answer should still not be below the exact FCI energy. The fact that low accuracy answers also happen is also a bit strange.

### What is happening and why is it wrong?

issues.title: Allow greater control over the dimension of the SCI subspace
issues.body:
### What should we add?

The [`solve_fermion`](https://github.com/Qiskit/qiskit-addon-sqd/blob/eedfcf980fb3ead067201b24ca169ccb36019f9e/qiskit_addon_sqd/fermion.py#L72) function accepts an array of bitstrings, where each bitstring has an "alpha" half and a "beta" half. In order to form the actual SCI subspace, these bitstrings are split into alpha and beta halves (this is done in [`bitstring_matrix_to_ci_strs`](https://github.com/Qiskit/qiskit-addon-sqd/blob/eedfcf980fb3ead067201b24ca169ccb36019f9e/qiskit_addon_sqd/fermion.py#L399)) and the actual subspace is formed as the cross product of the sets of unique alpha strings and unique beta strings. Furthermore, for closed-shell systems, the alpha and beta sets are actually merged, and the subspace formed as the cross product of the merged set with itself.

This procedure makes it difficult to directly control the subspace dimension, which is a useful feature. I'm not sure what we should do. Perhaps in hindsight, we should not have deprecated the [option](https://github.com/Qiskit/qiskit-addon-sqd/blob/eedfcf980fb3ead067201b24ca169ccb36019f9e/qiskit_addon_sqd/fermion.py#L114-L120) to pass the CI strings directly as input.

issues.body:
### Environment

- **qiskit-addon-sqd version**: 0.10.0
- **Python version**:  3.12.8
- **Operating system**: MacOS Sequoia 15.3.2


### What is happening and why is it wrong?

This is [line](https://github.com/Qiskit/qiskit-addon-sqd/blob/e4e802ef1daee45f78f023e58855a6081b5cdfd0/qiskit_addon_sqd/qubit.py#L294) in the function [`_int_conversion_from_bts_array`](https://github.com/Qiskit/qiskit-addon-sqd/blob/e4e802ef1daee45f78f023e58855a6081b5cdfd0/qiskit_addon_sqd/qubit.py#L281-L298) function initializes the variable `bitarray_asint` as `float` and then typecasts it to an integer. During this float to int typecasting, it may return incorrect results, especially for bitstrings corresponding to large integer value.


### How can we reproduce the issue?

Suppose our bitstring length is `60`, and it is composed of all `1` bits.

```
from qiskit_addon_sqd.qubit import _int_conversion_from_bts_array

def _int_conversion_from_bts_array_int64(bit_array: np.ndarray) -> Any:
    """Convert a bit array to an integer representation.

    NOTE: This can only handle up to 63 qubits. Then the integer will overflow

    Args:
        bit_array: A 1D array of ``bool`` representations of bit values.

    Returns:
        Integer representation of the bit array.

    """
    n_qubits = len(bit_array)
    bitarray_asint = np.int64(0)
    for i in range(n_qubits):
        bitarray_asint = bitarray_asint + bit_array[i] * 2 ** (n_qubits - 1 - i)

    return bitarray_asint.astype("longlong")  # type: ignore

# test bench
bitstring = "1" * 60
bit_array = np.array([True if bit == "1" else "False" for bit in bitstring])

val_from_orig_func = _int_conversion_from_bts_array(bit_array) # Output: 1152921504606846976
val_with_int64 = _int_conversion_from_bts_array_int64(bit_array) # Output: 1152921504606846975
str_to_int_python = int(bitstring, 2) # Output: 1152921504606846975

print(f">> Original:          {val_from_orig_func}")
print(f">> w/numpy.int64:     {val_with_int64}")
print(f">> Python str to int: {str_to_int_python}")
```
Output
```
>> Original:          1152921504606846976
>> w/numpy.int64:     1152921504606846975
>> Python str to int: 1152921504606846975
```
The current function with float to int typecasting return `1152921504606846976` where as native Python string to int conversion and `bitarray_asint = np.int64(0)` return `1152921504606846975`.

_No response_

```
bitarray_asint = np.int64(0)
```

issues.title: change probability weighting in configuration recovery
issues.body:
Change lines 174-184 in https://github.com/Qiskit/qiskit-addon-sqd/blob/main/qiskit_addon_sqd/configuration_recovery.py to
```
    if occ < ratio_exp:
        slope = (1.0 - eps) / ratio_exp
        return 1.0 - occ * slope

    # Occupancy is >= naive expectation.
    # Flip 1s to 0 with small (~eps) probability in this case
    if ratio_exp == 0.0:
        return 1 - eps
    slope = -eps / (1-ratio_exp)
    intercept = eps / (1-ratio_exp)
    return occ * slope + intercept
```

Why? This is a better heuristic for weighting probabilities to flip from 1->0, and is symmetric with the heuristic for weighting 0->1. With this scheme, we assign low weight (<eps) only when the target occupancy `occ` is greater than the actual mean occupancy `ratio_exp`, since in that case flipping a bit from 1->0 would only decrease the actual mean occupancy further. This makes more sense than the current version, which instead compares the target occupancy to 1 - actual mean occupancy.

### What should we add?

issues.body:
### What should we add?

Unfortunately, the SQD energy doesn't always decrease monotonically with configuration recovery iteration (for example, see the last figure in https://qiskit.github.io/qiskit-addon-sqd/tutorials/02_fermionic_lattice_hamiltonian.html). This can at least partially be attributed to the diagonalization in one iteration omitting some configurations that were important in the previous iteration. This can be alleviated by keeping important configurations (for example, those with coefficients whose absolute value is above a threshold) from one iteration to the next.

```python

    flattened = sci_state.amplitudes.reshape(-1)
    indices = np.argsort(np.abs(flattened))
    index = np.searchsorted(np.abs(flattened), carryover_threshold, sorter=indices)
    carryover_indices = indices[index:]
    alpha_indices, beta_indices = np.divmod(
        carryover_indices, sci_state.amplitudes.shape[1]
    )
    alpha_strings = sci_state.ci_strs_a[alpha_indices]
    beta_strings = sci_state.ci_strs_b[beta_indices]

issues.title: Rename "open_shell" argument and change default behavior
issues.body:
### What should we add?

The [`open_shell` argument](https://github.com/Qiskit/qiskit-addon-sqd/blob/d441dc4fa24c1b100c5d1236d5ed77fbc7427e01/qiskit_addon_sqd/fermion.py#L76) in `solve_fermion` and related functions is misleadingly named and, I think, has the wrong default behavior.
- The name suggests that setting it to True is only appropriate for open-shell systems, but this is not the case. It can also be used for closed-shell systems.
- The name does not describe what it actually does, which is to control whether to merge spin-alpha and spin-beta CI strings into a single list, so that the diagonalization subspace is invariant with respect to the exchange of spin alpha with spin beta.
- The default behavior, `open_shell=False`, is incompatible with the situation where the numbers of spin-alpha and spin-beta electrons differ. Because the `open_shell=True` behavior is applicable to all cases, it should be the default.

I propose to replace this option with an option called `symmetrize_spin`, which has the _opposite_ effect of the current `open_shell` argument. It should default to False. I've already done this for the function being introduced in https://github.com/Qiskit/qiskit-addon-sqd/pull/195.

https://qiskit.github.io/qiskit-addon-sqd/how_tos/select_open_closed_shell.html is affected.

issues.title: Get rid of samples_per_batch?
issues.body:
### What should we add?

`samples_per_batch` is not intuitive because its relation to the final subspace dimension is unclear. I have experimented with deterministic bitstring selection, which simply takes the most probable bitstrings, and it seems to work well. Here is some code:

```python
def _select_determinants(
    samples: dict[tuple[int, int], int | float],
    num: int,
    symmetrize_spin: bool,
    cartesian_product: bool,
) -> list[tuple[int, int]]:
    assert num >= 0
    if symmetrize_spin:
        samples = _canonicalize_samples(samples)
    dets = sorted(samples.keys(), key=lambda det: samples[det], reverse=True)
    result = []
    for a, b in dets:
        result.append((a, b))
        if symmetrize_spin and a != b:
            result.append((b, a))
        if len(result) >= num:
            break
    if cartesian_product:
        # use dict to emulate an ordered set
        dets_a = list(dict.fromkeys([a for (a, _) in result]))
        dets_b = list(dict.fromkeys([b for (_, b) in result]))
        if len(dets_a) * len(dets_b) > num:
            factor = math.sqrt(num / (len(dets_a) * len(dets_b)))
            dets_a = dets_a[: math.ceil(factor * len(dets_a))]
            dets_b = dets_b[: math.ceil(factor * len(dets_b))]
        result = list(itertools.product(dets_a, dets_b))
    return result


def _canonicalize_samples(samples: dict[tuple[int, int], int | float]):
    canonicalized = defaultdict(float)
    for det, count in samples.items():
        canonicalized[tuple(sorted(det))] += count
    return canonicalized
```

issues.title: Is it intended that symmetrize_spin costs 4x for <1 nHa here, while spin_sq never gets set on the default path?
issues.body:
### What should we add?

Some of this bears on #203, which is still open.

I've been running the shipped pipeline on the [2Fe-2S] and [4Fe-4S] systems from the Sci. Adv. 2025 study and hit a defaults question the docs don't settle. Everything below comes from the standard configuration-recovery loop on 10⁶ samples drawn from a converged benchmark state.

`symmetrize_spin=True` vs `False`:

- ground-state energy difference: under 1 nanohartree, every batch of every iteration
- subspace dimension: 4.00x larger (194,481 vs 48,600 determinants at iteration 4)

So on these systems it's pure cost. I don't think the implementation is wrong; as far as I can tell it does what it documents. Completion makes spin symmetry representable in the subspace, but nothing downstream selects for it, and in the ground manifold the S² block comes out proportional to the identity. It permits a singlet without ever producing one.

The package's own `spin_square()` on the result gives ⟨S²⟩ = 4.84 after 4 recovery iterations (3-batch mean; 4.83 on the best single batch). Target for these systems is a singlet at 0, so that's not a near miss; it isn't any pure spin state.

Meanwhile `solve_sci` and `solve_sci_batch` both take a keyword-only `spin_sq` (default `None`) that feeds `fix_spin_(myci, ss=spin_sq)` and would target a spin sector directly. But `diagonalize_fermionic_hamiltonian` has no `spin_sq` parameter, and with `sci_solver=None` it calls the batch solver positionally:

```python
sci_solver(ci_strings, one_body_tensor, two_body_tensor, norb, nelec)
```

so `spin_sq` stays `None` on every default-path run. It's reachable through `functools.partial(solve_sci_batch, spin_sq=0.0)` and I've used it that way, so I'm not claiming anything is broken. What I can't tell is whether the pairing is deliberate: the spin option surfaced at top level doesn't target spin, and the one that does isn't surfaced.

I've read #248, which asked for general `**kwargs` forwarding here and was closed as not planned, so I'm not re-litigating that. #308 asks for `shift` on `solve_sci`, which is the same `fix_spin_` family. Both are why I'm asking rather than opening a PR.

Two questions:

1. Is `symmetrize_spin` meant to improve the spin character of the returned state, or only to make the symmetric sector representable? The docstring reads like the former to me and the measurement matches the latter. If it's the latter, I'm happy to send a docs PR saying so, with these numbers in it.
2. Given #248, is `functools.partial(solve_sci_batch, spin_sq=...)` simply the intended way to target a spin sector from the top-level driver? A one-line "yes, that's the pattern" is a complete answer and I'll document it.

On #203: `open_shell` is still on `solve_fermion`, `optimize_orbitals` and `bitstring_matrix_to_ci_strs` (`fermion.py:543`, `:647`, `:795`) while the newer driver has moved to `symmetrize_spin`. Rather than add another opinion about the naming, treat the above as measurements of what the current default actually produces on a published benchmark.

Version: qiskit-addon-sqd 0.12.1. Full measurements, harness and raw data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21359923, out of a spin audit of these benchmarks preprinted at https://doi.org/10.26434/chemrxiv.15006382/v1. If I've misconfigured something, name the configuration and I'll rerun it and post the result here either way.

- Tyler Vitale, Pure State Labs

issues.title: solve_sci with spin_sq set returns converged=False on every cold-started arm tested
issues.body:
Tested on 0.12.1 (also present at 0.3.0).

Passing `spin_sq` to `solve_sci` wires PySCF's `fix_spin_`. Cold-started, that path did not converge on any arm I ran:

- 5 of 5 `(subspace, shift, max_cycle)` arms returned `converged = False`
- shifts 0.1 and 0.2, at the silent default `max_cycle` and again at `max_cycle = 600`
- each landed 0.27 to 0.33 Ha above the true penalized minimum for that subspace

The minimum itself is fine. Handing the same kernel an independently converged penalized ground state as its initial guess returns `converged = True`, overlap 1.000000, and the same penalized Rayleigh quotient to machine precision. So this looks like an initial-guess pathology rather than a disagreement about where the minimum is.

**Why it seems worth fixing:** `converged = False` comes back without raising, so a caller who does not check the flag gets a silently wrong answer from the one spin-targeting option the package exposes. The subspaces here were the package's own converged product spaces from `diagonalize_fermionic_hamiltonian`, so this is reachable on a normal path.

**Reproducer:** `_sqdpen_s3b.py` in https://github.com/PureStateLabs/sqd-spin-referee (archive `sqdpen_s3b.npz` has the five arms and the seeded confirmation).

**Possible fixes:** warn or raise when `converged = False` comes back, and/or seed the penalized solve from the unpenalized ground state, which is already in hand at that point.

Possibly related to #308.

issues.title: solve_fermion's default max_cycle can return an under-converged result with no warning at large subspace dimension
issues.body:
At subspace dimension 5.625e7 (7500 x 7500 product space, [2Fe-2S] MO integrals), `solve_fermion` at the default `max_cycle` returns without any warning at a residual far short of convergence. Raising `max_cycle` to 400 changes the returned energy materially. The default is the only knob I had to touch to get a usable result at that dimension.

There is a sharper version of this that may be worth a warning in its own right. In a dense near-degenerate manifold the **energy** converges long before the **state** does. Tightening the residual from 3.5e-4 to 6.0e-5 on that subspace moved the energy by 1.9 microhartree, and moved the returned `spin_square()` from 1.287 to 1.371. Tightening a further 18.6x left the energy flat and the spin value stable at 1.3711.

So a caller who reads `SCIState.spin_square()` off a vector that stopped early gets a spin value that looks trustworthy because the energy looks stable, and the energy is not diagnostic of whether the eigenvector has settled.

**Suggestion:** emit a warning when the iteration cap is reached without meeting tolerance, and surface the final residual on the returned object so callers can compare it against the local gap.

Happy to send a PR for the warning if that is a change you would take.

issues.title: symmetrize_spin quadruples the subspace with no measurable effect on spin-mixed input
issues.body:
Not a correctness complaint, and it is consistent with the docstring wording in #338. Flagging the cost, because it is 4x the determinants and it is not obvious from the API when it will do nothing.

Measured on 1e6 samples drawn from a converged [2Fe-2S] selected-CI vector (D = 170,448, spin-mixed, the kind of state this protocol actually produces), running `diagonalize_fermionic_hamiltonian` with `symmetrize_spin=True` against `False` at otherwise identical knobs:

- every batch of every recovery iteration agrees to **dE < 1e-9 Ha** and **d<S^2> ~ 1e-11**
- the symmetrized subspace is exactly **4.00x larger**: 194,481 vs 48,600 determinants at iteration 4

The mechanism is measurable: the added spin-image determinants are H-uncoupled from the converged ground at the solve's own residual scale (||P+ H v|| <= 2.5e-9 Ha across 14 completion checkpoints), so they take essentially zero variational weight and the ground state persists unchanged.

It is not a no-op everywhere. On low-<S^2> input (raw hardware shots and noiseless template samples) it does act, and buys 7.7 to 9.5 mHa. The cases where it changes nothing and the cases where it helps look separable in advance by the input's spin character.

**Reproducers:** `_sqdship_delta.py` in https://github.com/PureStateLabs/sqd-spin-referee, and a browser-only version at https://colab.research.google.com/github/PureStateLabs/sqd-spin-referee/blob/main/verify_sqd_spin.ipynb

**Suggestion:** a line in the docstring noting the 4x subspace cost and that it can leave spin-mixed input unchanged would save people the run.

pullRequests.title: Support bitstrings longer than 72 bits by removing array2string usage
pullRequests.body:
array2string starts to add a newline when the bitstring is longer than 73 bits.

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng()
bitstring = rng.integers(2, size=74, dtype=bool)
np.array2string(bitstring.astype(int), separator="")[1:-1]
```
```
'0010011001100011100000000001100100000101001111001000000111011101001111011\n 0'
```

The code in this PR is correct, simpler, and also much faster.

pullRequests.title: Bump mypy from 1.11.2 to 1.13.0
pullRequests.body:
Bumps [mypy](https://github.com/python/mypy) from 1.11.2 to 1.13.0.
Changelog

Sourced from mypy's changelog.

Mypy Release Notes

Next release

Change to enum membership semantics

As per the updated typing specification for enums, enum members must be left unannotated.

class Pet(Enum):
    CAT = 1  # Member attribute
    DOG = 2  # Member attribute
    WOLF: int = 3  # New error: Enum members must be left unannotated

species: str  # Considered a non-member attribute

In particular, the specification change can result in issues in type stubs (.pyi files), since historically it was common to leave the value absent:

# In a type stub (.pyi file)

class Pet(Enum):

# Change in semantics: previously considered members, now non-member attributes

CAT: int

DOG: int


# Mypy will now issue a warning if it detects this situation in type stubs:
# > Detected enum "Pet" in a type stub with zero members.
# > There is a chance this is due to a recent change in the semantics of enum membership.
# > If so, use `member = value` to mark an enum member, instead of `member: type`



class Pet(Enum):

# As per the specification, you should now do one of the following:

DOG = 1  # Member attribute with value 1 and known type

WOLF = cast(int, ...)  # Member attribute with unknown value but known type

LION = ...  # Member attribute with unknown value and unknown type

Contributed by Terence Honles in PR 17207 and Shantanu Jain in PR 18068.

Mypy 1.13

We’ve just uploaded mypy 1.13 to the Python Package Index (PyPI). Mypy is a static type checker for Python. You can install it as follows:

python3 -m pip install -U mypy

pullRequests.title: Add a linter to check the images' alt text
pullRequests.body:
In order to meet the [IBM Accessibility Requirements](https://www.ibm.com/able/requirements/requirements) for the API docs, we need to ensure that all images have appropriate alt text so that users can understand any meaningful visuals. The alt text should serve the same purpose as the images on the page, conveying the same meaning rather than describing visual characteristics. In addition, if an image contains important words for understanding the content, the alt text should include those words as well.

This PR adds a linter to check that all images have alt text. The current invalid images, if any, have been included in an allowlist that will help us to not break CI before the text is added.

If the script detects an image without alt text, it will show an error indicating the file where the image is located and the line where we are using a sphinx directive like `.. image::` or `.. plot::` that generates an image. Example:

```
💔 Some images are missing the alt text

Errors found in qiskit_ibm_runtime/fake_provider/__init__.py:
- Error in line 34: .. plot::

Alt text is crucial for making documentation accessible to all users. It should serve the same purpose as the images on the page, conveying the same meaning rather than describing visual characteristics. When an image contains words that are important to understanding the content, the alt text should include those words as well.
```

To fix the error, the `:alt: [Your text here]` option must be added under the lines indicated in the error messages. However, If the `.. plot::` directive is used, but no image is generated, you can use the option `:nofigs:`.

pullRequests.title: Bump mypy from 1.13.0 to 1.14.1
pullRequests.body:
Bumps [mypy](https://github.com/python/mypy) from 1.13.0 to 1.14.1.
Changelog

Sourced from mypy's changelog.

Mypy Release Notes

Next release

Drop Support for Python 3.8

Mypy no longer supports running with Python 3.8, which has reached end-of-life. When running mypy with Python 3.9+, it is still possible to type check code that needs to support Python 3.8 with the --python-version 3.8 argument. Support for this will be dropped in the first half of 2025!

Contributed by Marc Mueller (PR 17492).

Mypyc accelerated mypy wheels for aarch64

Mypy can compile itself to C extension modules using mypyc. This makes mypy 3-5x faster than if mypy is interpreted with pure Python. We now build and upload mypyc accelerated mypy wheels for manylinux_aarch64 to PyPI, making it easy for users on such platforms to realise this speedup.

Contributed by Christian Bundy (PR mypy_mypyc-wheels#76)

--strict-bytes

By default, mypy treats an annotation of bytes as permitting bytearray and memoryview. PEP 688 specified the removal of this special case. Use this flag to disable this behavior. --strict-bytes will be enabled by default in mypy 2.0.

Contributed by Ali Hamdan (PR 18137) and Shantanu Jain (PR 13952).

Improvements to partial type handling in loops

This change results in mypy better modelling control flow within loops and hence detecting several issues it previously did not detect. In some cases, this change may require use of an additional explicit annotation of a variable.

Contributed by Christoph Tyralla (PR 18180).

(Speaking of partial types, another reminder that mypy plans on enabling --local-partial-types by default in mypy 2.0).

Mypy 1.14

We’ve just uploaded mypy 1.14 to the Python Package Index (PyPI). Mypy is a static type checker for Python. This release includes new features and bug fixes. You can install it as follows:

python3 -m pip install -U mypy

pullRequests.body:
Bumps [mypy](https://github.com/python/mypy) from 1.14.1 to 1.15.0.
Changelog

Sourced from mypy's changelog.

Mypy Release Notes

Next Release

Different Property Getter and Setter Types

Mypy now supports using different types for property getter and setter.

class A:
    value: int

@property
def f(self) -> int:
    return self.value
@f.setter
def f(self, x: str | int) -> None:
    try:
        self.value = int(x)
    except ValueError:
        raise Exception(f"'{x}' is not a valid value for 'f'")

Contributed by Ivan Levkivskyi (PR 18510)

Selectively Disable Deprecated Warnings

It's now possible to selectively disable warnings generated from warnings.deprecated using the --deprecated-calls-exclude option.

# mypy --enable-error-code deprecated
#      --deprecated-calls-exclude=foo.A
import foo

foo.A().func()  # OK, the deprecated warning is ignored


file foo.py


from typing_extensions import deprecated

class A:

@​deprecated("Use A.func2 instead")

def func(self): pass

pullRequests.body:
Bumps [mypy](https://github.com/python/mypy) from 1.15.0 to 1.16.0.
Changelog

Sourced from mypy's changelog.

Mypy Release Notes

Next Release

Mypy 1.16

We’ve just uploaded mypy 1.16 to the Python Package Index (PyPI). Mypy is a static type checker for Python. This release includes new features and bug fixes. You can install it as follows:

python3 -m pip install -U mypy

You can read the full documentation for this release on Read the Docs.

Different Property Getter and Setter Types

Mypy now supports using different types for a property getter and setter:

class A:
    _value: int

@property
def foo(self) -> int:
    return self._value

@foo.setter
def foo(self, x: str | int) -> None:
    try:
        self._value = int(x)
    except ValueError:
        raise Exception(f"'{x}' is not a valid value for 'foo'")

This was contributed by Ivan Levkivskyi (PR 18510).

Flexible Variable Redefinitions (Experimental)

Mypy now allows unannotated variables to be freely redefined with different types when using the experimental --allow-redefinition-new flag. You will also need to enable --local-partial-types. Mypy will now infer a union type when different types are assigned to a variable:

# mypy: allow-redefinition-new, local-partial-types

def f(n: int, b: bool) -> int | str:
if b:
x = n

pullRequests.title: Test that diagonalize_fermionic_hamiltonian result is reproducible with random seed
Add max_dim argument to diagonalize_fermionic_hamiltonian
pullRequests.body:
Fixes #https://github.com/Qiskit/qiskit-addon-sqd/issues/148

The maximum dimension is given as a pair `(max_dim_a, max_dim_b)` (you can just specify a single integer if you want them to be the same). In each iteration, the bitstrings are picked in this order, until the maximum dimension is reached:
- Explicitly requested bitstrings
- Carryover bitstrings. If there are more carryover bitstrings than we can pick without exceeding the maximum dimension, we pick them randomly (uniformly without replacement).
- Bitstrings sampled from the QPU. If there are more sampled bitstrings than we can pick without exceeding the maximum dimension, we pick them randomly (uniformly without replacement).

pullRequests.title: Reduce code duplication in `_p_flip_1_to_0`
pullRequests.body:
In #185, the `_p_flip_1_to_0` function was updated with the goal of having it be symmetric with the `_p_flip_0_to_1` function.

However, there are some corner cases that are not symmetric yet, such as the following:

```python
>>> from qiskit_addon_sqd.configuration_recovery import _p_flip_0_to_1, _p_flip_1_to_0
>>> _p_flip_1_to_0(0.1, 0.3)
0.0077777777777777776
>>> _p_flip_0_to_1(0.9, 0.7)
0.007777777777777777
>>> _p_flip_1_to_0(0, 0.3)
0.99
>>> _p_flip_0_to_1(1, 0.7)
0.006999999999999999
```

This PR changes `_p_flip_1_to_0` to simply call `_p_flip_0_to_1` with the appropriate parameters, which simplifies (don't repeat yourself) and fixes the above discrepancy.  The output following this change is:

```python
>>> from qiskit_addon_sqd.configuration_recovery import _p_flip_0_to_1, _p_flip_1_to_0
>>> _p_flip_1_to_0(0.1, 0.3)
0.007777777777777777
>>> _p_flip_0_to_1(0.9, 0.7)
0.007777777777777777
>>> _p_flip_1_to_0(0, 0.3)
0.006999999999999999
>>> _p_flip_0_to_1(1, 0.7)
0.006999999999999999
```

This change also fixes #244.

pullRequests.title: Use wheel for tox testing
pullRequests.body:
This changes the tox configuration to build a wheel and use that wheel for testing, similar to how we do it in the other addons.

It is important to ensure that the wheel itself is used during testing rather than the `qiskit_addon_sqd` local directory, as the latter will not automatically have the compiled code available.  So, to restore the ability to run `tox -e py` from the root directory of the repository, this PR moves all python source files to a directory called `python`. This is a layout [recommended by the maturin docs](https://www.maturin.rs/project_layout.html#mixed-rustpython-project) and is also the one used by ffsim.  This structure provides the benefits of a [`src`
layout](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/discussions/src-layout-vs-flat-layout/).

One nice thing about the new directory structure is that many of the lines in `tox.ini` now say `python/` instead of `qiskit_addon_sqd/`. So, if other addons were to adopt this change, then their `tox.ini` files would look even more alike, which could be good for maintainability.

This also bumps the versions of numpy and pyo3 to 0.26.  I cannot remember at this point whether it was absolutely necessary, and if desired I could try to separate out this change.

pullRequests.title: Bump mypy from 1.18.2 to 1.19.0
pullRequests.body:
Bumps [mypy](https://github.com/python/mypy) from 1.18.2 to 1.19.0.
Changelog

Sourced from mypy's changelog.

Mypy Release Notes

Next Release

Drop Support for Python 3.9

Mypy no longer supports running with Python 3.9, which has reached end-of-life. When running mypy with Python 3.10+, it is still possible to type check code that needs to support Python 3.9 with the --python-version 3.9 argument. Support for this will be dropped in the first half of 2026!

Contributed by Marc Mueller (PR 20156).

Mypy 1.19

We’ve just uploaded mypy 1.19.0 to the Python Package Index (PyPI). Mypy is a static type checker for Python. This release includes new features, performance improvements and bug fixes. You can install it as follows:

python3 -m pip install -U mypy

You can read the full documentation for this release on Read the Docs.

Python 3.9 Support Ending Soon

This is the last mypy feature release that supports Python 3.9, which reached end of life in October 2025.

Performance Improvements

  • Switch to a more dynamic SCC processing logic (Ivan Levkivskyi, PR 20053)
  • Speed up type aliases (Ivan Levkivskyi, PR 19810)

Fixed‑Format Cache Improvements

Mypy uses a cache by default to speed up incremental runs by reusing partial results from earlier runs. Mypy 1.18 added a new binary fixed-format cache representation as an experimental feature. The feature is no longer experimental, and we are planning to enable it by default in a future mypy release (possibly 1.20), since it's faster and uses less space than the original, JSON-based cache format. Use --fixed-format-cache to enable the fixed-format cache.

Mypy now has an extra dependency on the librt PyPI package, as it's needed for cache serialization and deserialization.

Mypy ships with a tool to convert fixed-format cache files to the old JSON format. Example of how to use this:

$ python -m mypy.exportjson .mypy_cache/.../my_module.data.ff

Changelog

Mypy Release Notes

Next Release

Mypy 1.20

We’ve just uploaded mypy 1.20.0 to the Python Package Index (PyPI). Mypy is a static type checker for Python. This release includes new features, performance improvements and bug fixes. You can install it as follows:

python3 -m pip install -U mypy

You can read the full documentation for this release on Read the Docs.

Planned Changes to Defaults and Flags in Mypy 2.0

As a reminder, we are planning to enable --local-partial-types by default in mypy 2.0, which will likely be the next feature release. This will often require at least minor code changes. This option is implicitly enabled by mypy daemon, so this makes the behavior of daemon and non-daemon modes consistent.

Note that this release improves the compatibility of --local-partial-types significantly to make the switch easier (see below for more).

This can also be configured in a mypy configuration file (use False to disable):

local_partial_types = True

For more information, refer to the documentation.

We will also enable --strict-bytes by default in mypy 2.0. This usually requires at most minor code changes to adopt. For more information, refer to the documentation.

Finally, --allow-redefinition-new will be renamed to --allow-redefinition. If you want to continue using the older --allow-redefinition semantics which are less flexible (e.g. limited support for conditional redefinitions), you can switch to --allow-redefinition-old, which is currently supported as an alias to the legacy --allow-redefinition behavior. To use --allow-redefinition in the upcoming mypy 2.0, you can't use --no-local-partial-types. For more information, refer to the documentation.

pullRequests.title: Add official support for Python 3.13
pullRequests.body:
## Summary

Adds official support for Python 3.13, following the same pattern used when earlier Python versions were added/dropped (e.g. #256, #83) and matching the configuration of sibling addons such as `qiskit-addon-utils` (which already supports 3.13).

## Changes

- **`pyproject.toml`**: add the `Programming Language :: Python :: 3.13` classifier.
- **`tox.ini`**: extend the `envlist` and the notebook test environment factors to include `py313`.
- **`.github/workflows/test_latest_versions.yml`**: add `3.13` to the matrix and bump the macOS job to `3.13`.
- **`.github/workflows/test_development_versions.yml`**: add `3.13` to the matrix (replacing the previous newest `3.12`).
- **`releasenotes/notes/add-py313-*.yaml`**: release note announcing the new support.

`requires-python` already reads `>=3.10`, so no change is needed there.

## Notes for reviewers

The macOS and development-version newest-Python jobs were bumped from 3.12 → 3.13 to keep testing on the newest supported version, consistent with `qiskit-addon-utils`. Let me know if you'd prefer to keep an explicit 3.12 macOS/dev entry instead.

Adds official support for Python 3.14, following the same pattern as the recently merged Python 3.13 PR (#309).

## Changes

- **`pyproject.toml`**: add the `Programming Language :: Python :: 3.14` classifier.
- **`tox.ini`**: extend the `envlist` and the notebook test environment factors to include `py314`.
- **`.github/workflows/test_latest_versions.yml`**: add `3.14` to the matrix and bump the macOS job to `3.14`.
- **`.github/workflows/test_development_versions.yml`**: bump the newest matrix entry from `3.13` to `3.14`.
- **`releasenotes/notes/add-py313-*.yaml`**: updated the existing 3.13 release note to also announce 3.14, rather than adding a separate note.

`requires-python` already reads `>=3.10`, so no change is needed there.

## Notes for reviewers

As with the 3.13 PR, the macOS and development-version newest-Python jobs were bumped to `3.14` to keep testing on the newest supported version.

Bumps [mypy](https://github.com/python/mypy) from 1.20.0 to 2.1.0.
Changelog

Sourced from mypy's changelog.

Mypy Release Notes

Next Release

Mypy 2.1

We’ve just uploaded mypy 2.1.0 to the Python Package Index (PyPI). Mypy is a static type checker for Python. This release includes new features, performance improvements and bug fixes. You can install it as follows:

python3 -m pip install -U mypy

You can read the full documentation for this release on Read the Docs.

librt.vecs: Fast Growable Array Type for Mypyc

The new librt.vecs module provides an efficient growable array type vec that is optimized for mypyc use. It provides fast, packed arrays with integer and floating point value types, which can be several times faster than list, and tens of times faster than array.array in code compiled using mypyc. It also supports nested vec objects and non-value-type items, such as vec[vec[str]].

Refer to the documentation for the details.

Contributed by Jukka Lehtosalo.

librt.random: Fast Pseudo-Random Number Generation

The new librt.random module provides fast pseudo-random number generation that is optimized for code compiled using mypyc. It can be 3x to 10x faster than the stdlib random module in compiled code.

Refer to the documentation for the details.

Contributed by Jukka Lehtosalo (PR 21433).

Mypyc Improvements

  • Enable incremental self-compilation (Vaggelis Danias, PR 21369)

pullRequests.title: Refactor diagonalize_fermionic_hamiltonian loop body into helper functions
pullRequests.body:
## Summary

Splits the two large regions of the configuration recovery loop in `diagonalize_fermionic_hamiltonian` into helper functions:

- `_prepare_ci_strings` — configuration recovery / postselection, subsampling, and CI-string construction (returns the batch of `ci_strings`).
- `_process_results` — best-result update, convergence check, and carryover-string computation, returning a bundled `_IterationState`.

The loop body is now a flat, one-level-deep sequence: prepare → solve → callback → process. The mid-loop convergence `break` becomes a `converged` flag on the returned state.

## Why

This is a pure, behavior-preserving refactor that establishes cleaner seams in the loop. It is groundwork for the SPMD/MPI work in #329: with these helpers in place, the distributed version reduces to wrapping the two helper calls in a control-process check and broadcasting the single `_IterationState`, rather than deeply nesting the whole loop body and broadcasting several separate variables.

## Verification

- `tox -e lint` passes (mypy clean).
- `tox -e py` passes (21 tests).
- The extracted code was moved verbatim; a line-for-line comparison against the previous loop body shows the only differences are the `break` becoming a `converged` flag and the `sci_solver`/`callback` calls remaining inline in the main function.

Released on 2026-07-23.

Check out the blog post for a migration guide and overview of the changes!

Breaking changes

  • Ruff now enables a much larger set of rules by default (413, up from 59). See the blog post for more details and the new Default Rules page for a full listing of the enabled rules. Note that this is primarily an expansion, but 18 of the more opinionated pycodestyle (E) and pyflakes (F) rules have been removed from the default set: E401, E402, E701, E702, E703, E711, E712, E713, E714, E721, E731, E741, E742, E743, F403, F405, F406, and F722.

  • Ruff can now format Python code blocks in Markdown files and will do this by default. See the documentation for more details.

  • Ruff now supports ruff: ignore comments at the ends of lines, like noqa comments, or on the line preceding a diagnostic. For example, these both suppress an unused-import (F401) diagnostic:

    import math  # ruff: ignore[F401]

    ruff: ignore[F401]
    

    import os

  • Fixes are now shown in check and format --check output:

    ❯ ruff format --check .
unformatted: File would be reformatted
 --> try.md:1:1
  |
1 | ```python
  - import   math
2 + import math
3 | ```
  |

    1 file would be reformatted

    This example also shows off the Markdown formatting.

  • format --check now supports the same output formats as the linter, including the github and gitlab outputs for rendering annotations in CI:

    ❯ ruff format --check --output-format github .
::error title=ruff (unformatted),file=try.md,line=2,col=8,endLine=2,endColumn=10::try.md:2:8: unformatted: File would be reformatted

    See the CLI help or documentation for the full list of supported formats.

  • The filename, location, end_location, fix.edits[].location, and fix.edits[].end_location fields in the JSON output format may now be null rather than defaulting to the empty string and row 1, column 1, respectively.

pullRequests.title: Bump mypy from 2.1.0 to 2.3.0
pullRequests.body:
Bumps [mypy](https://github.com/python/mypy) from 2.1.0 to 2.3.0.
Changelog

Sourced from mypy's changelog.

Mypy Release Notes

Next Release

Packaging changes

  • No longer provide mypyc-accelerated wheels for macOS x86_64 [mypyc-wheels #119](mypyc/mypy_mypyc-wheels#119)

Mypy 2.3

We've just uploaded mypy 2.3.0 to the Python Package Index (PyPI). Mypy is a static type checker for Python. This release includes new features, performance improvements and bug fixes. You can install it as follows:

python3 -m pip install -U mypy

You can read the full documentation for this release on Read the Docs.

The Upcoming Switch to the New Native Parser

We are planning to enable the new native parser (--native-parser) by default soon. We recommend that you test the native parser in your projects and report any issues in the mypy issue tracker.

Mypyc Free-threading Memory Safety

Free-threaded Python builds that don't have the GIL require additional synchronization primitives or lock-free algorithms to ensure memory safety when there are race conditions (for example, when a thread reads a list item while another thread writes the same list item concurrently). This release greatly improves memory safety of free threading.

List operations are now memory-safe on free threaded Python builds, even in the presence of race conditions. This has some performance cost. For list-heavy workloads, using librt.vecs.vec instead of list is often significantly faster, but note that vec is not (and likely won't be) fully memory safe, and the user is expected to avoid race conditions. The newly introduced librt.threading.Lock helps with this. Using variable-length tuples can also be more efficient than lists, since tuples are immutable and don't require expensive synchronization to ensure memory safety.

Instance attribute access is also (mostly) memory safe now on free-threaded builds in the presence of race conditions. We are planning to fix the remaining unsafe cases in a future release.

Full list of changes:

  • Make attribute access memory safe on free-threaded builds (Jukka Lehtosalo, PR 21705)
  • Fix unsafe borrowing of instance attributes with free-threading (Jukka Lehtosalo, PR 21688)
  • Make list get/set item more memory safe on free-threaded builds (Jukka Lehtosalo, PR 21683)
  • Don't borrow list items on free-threaded builds (Jukka Lehtosalo, PR 21679)
  • Make multiple assignment from list memory-safe on free-threaded builds (Jukka Lehtosalo, PR 21684)

pullRequests.title: Accept NumPy bitstrings in fermionic diagonalization
pullRequests.body:
Closes #265.

`diagonalize_fermionic_hamiltonian` now accepts sampled bitstrings as either a Qiskit `BitArray` or a two-dimensional NumPy boolean array.

NumPy samples are deduplicated and converted to empirical probabilities in the same way as `BitArray` samples. The tests cover both representations and exercise the NumPy input through the full diagonalization path.

Tests:
- `pytest test/`
- Ruff formatting and lint checks
- Pylint
- `reno lint`

Enable coverage CI workflow and set fail-under to 75%
pullRequests.body:
This PR was generated by Claude Opus 5 under my guidance.

<hr>

### Enable the coverage workflow

`.github/workflows/README.md` has documented a `coverage.yml` workflow all along, but the workflow file itself was never actually added to this repo — so `tox -e coverage` has never run in CI here. This brings the workflow over from `qiskit-addon-utils` verbatim, along with the matching Coveralls badge in the README.

### Lower `fail_under` from 100 to 75

Coverage currently sits at **77%**, so a `fail_under` of 100 was unachievable and the environment would have failed immediately on being enabled. Lowering the threshold to 75% in both `tox.ini` and `pyproject.toml` makes the workflow reflect the actual state of the test suite while still guarding against regressions from here.

Current per-module breakdown:

```
Name                                         Stmts   Miss Branch BrPart  Cover
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
qiskit_addon_sqd/__init__.py                     0      0      0      0   100%
qiskit_addon_sqd/configuration_recovery.py      78      0     26      2    98%
qiskit_addon_sqd/counts.py                      67      0     24      0   100%
qiskit_addon_sqd/fermion.py                    344    121     76     11    61%
qiskit_addon_sqd/processes.py                   41     13      6      2    64%
qiskit_addon_sqd/qubit.py                       59      0     10      0   100%
qiskit_addon_sqd/subsampling.py                 58      3     28      3    93%
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
TOTAL                                          647    137    170     18    77%
```

`fermion.py` and `processes.py` are where the gap lives. Raising the threshold back toward 100 is worth doing incrementally as those get covered, but that's out of scope here.

### Note on the badge

The Coveralls badge (and the upload step at the end of the workflow) will only render real numbers once the Coveralls integration is enabled for `Qiskit/qiskit-addon-sqd`. Until then the badge will show "unknown" — the upload step is `if: always()` and won't fail the job.

pullRequests.title: Remove verbose kwarg from fulqrum calls in integration guide
pullRequests.body:
This PR was generated by Claude Opus 5 under my guidance.

<hr>

Fulqrum removed the `verbose` keyword argument from `SubspaceHamiltonian.to_csr_linearoperator_fast()` (along with `to_csr_linearoperator()`, `_to_linearoperator()`, and `diagonal_vector()`) in [`60bc326`](https://github.com/qiskit-community/fulqrum/commit/60bc326427ec86ec687c57480ce9f5df16c3891a), so passing `verbose=False` now raises a `TypeError`.

This drops the argument from the two `to_csr_linearoperator_fast()` call sites in `docs/guides/integrate_fulqrum.ipynb`. The `diagonal_vector()` calls in that notebook already pass no arguments, so they needed no change.

The development-versions test workflow builds fulqrum from `main`, so that job exercises the notebook against the updated signature. The `fulqrum` extra in `pyproject.toml` is still pinned to an older commit; since the argument was optional in that version, the notebook works with both.

v4.0.8

What's new in Pylint 4.0.8?

Release date: 2026-08-29

False Positives Fixed

  • Fix a false positive for :ref:unspecified-encoding when an open call uses a mode argument that cannot be inferred.

    Closes #10201

  • Fix a false positive for invalid-name (C0103) on names assigned in an if __name__ == "__main__": block. Such a block reads like a script body, so a name there is now accepted if it matches either the constant or the variable naming style.

    Closes #10766

  • Fix false positives for :ref:invalid-str-returned, :ref:invalid-repr-returned, :ref:invalid-format-returned, :ref:invalid-bytes-returned, :ref:invalid-hash-returned, :ref:invalid-index-returned, :ref:invalid-length-returned, :ref:invalid-length-hint-returned, :ref:invalid-getnewargs-returned and :ref:invalid-getnewargs-ex-returned when the returned value is an instance of a subclass of the expected builtin type, such as self in a str subclass or a namedtuple.

    Closes #11306

  • Fix false positives for :ref:bad-string-format-type when the argument is an instance of a subclass of int, float or str, such as bool or an IntEnum member formatted with %d.

    Closes #11315

False Negatives Fixed

  • redundant-unittest-assert now also flags assertEqual and assertNotEqual when both compared values are constants, e.g. self.assertEqual(5, 5).

I'd also like to thank my employer, Dropbox, for supporting mypy development.

Mypy 2.2

We've just uploaded mypy 2.2.0 to the Python Package Index (PyPI). Mypy is a static type checker for Python. This release includes new features, performance improvements and bug fixes. You can install it as follows:

python3 -m pip install -U mypy

You can read the full documentation for this release on Read the Docs.

Support for Closed TypedDicts (PEP 728)

Mypy now supports closed TypedDicts as specified in PEP 728. A closed TypedDict cannot have extra keys beyond those explicitly defined. This allows the type checker to determine that certain operations are safe when they otherwise wouldn't be due to the potential presence of unknown keys.

You can use the closed keyword argument with TypedDict:

HasName = TypedDict("HasName", {"name": str})
HasOnlyName = TypedDict("HasOnlyName", {"name": str}, closed=True)
Movie = TypedDict("Movie", {"name": str, "year": int})

movie: Movie = {"name": "Nimona", "year": 2023}
has_name: HasName = movie  # OK: HasName is open (default)
has_only_name: HasOnlyName = movie  # Error: HasOnlyName is closed and Movie has extra "year" key
</tr></table>

pullRequests.title: add release note for bumping Qiskit to 2.0
Cap Fulqrum guide subspace in CI to avoid notebook OOM
pullRequests.body:
## Summary

`docs/guides/integrate_fulqrum.ipynb` can fail in CI (`tox -e notebook`) with:

```
FulqrumError: 'Sparse matrix copy of size 796.911 Mb does not fit within available memory.'
```

We had not seen this OOM until it surfaced on #373 (the C++ `recover_configurations` acceleration). That change does **not** make the recovered subspace larger: running this notebook's seeded SQD loop with each backend and recording the subspace dimension per iteration gives essentially identical sizes (max ≈ 413,449 for C++ vs ≈ 412,164 for pure Python — a 0.3% difference, with the per-iteration trajectories tracking closely). What differs is *which* configurations the different random stream recovers, which shifted this run's peak allocation just enough to tip an already-marginal case over the runner's memory ceiling. In short, the notebook was always sitting near the limit; #373 exposed it.

The underlying reason the notebook sits near the ceiling is that it runs its SQD workflow with an **unbounded subspace** (no `max_dim`). That is the honest, general example we want on the documentation site — and it is what a reader copies — but executing it that way exhausts memory on a CI runner, because Fulqrum materializes the projected Hamiltonian as a sparse (CSR) matrix (~797 MB copy) for the fast diagonalization path.

## Approach

Rather than bake a `max_dim` into the published notebook (which readers would copy and inherit a cap that is wrong for their own problem), this caps the subspace **for CI execution only**:

- `tools/ci_cap_notebook_memory.py` injects `max_dim=300` into the notebook's `diagonalize_fermionic_hamiltonian` calls **in the working-tree copy**.
- Each notebook-testing workflow (`test_latest_versions`, `test_minimum_versions`, `test_development_versions`) runs it as a step before `tox`.
- The change is never committed. The docs build does not execute notebooks (`nbsphinx_execute = "never"`), so the **published notebook and its saved outputs stay unbounded** — the site is unaffected.

The injector is strict: it asserts it edited exactly the expected number of calls and exits non-zero otherwise, so a future refactor of the notebook cannot silently reintroduce the out-of-memory failure.

## Why not the alternatives

- **Matrix-free** (`Hsub` passed directly instead of `to_csr_linearoperator_fast()`) is correct — it produces an identical energy — but ~22× slower on this problem (measured ~1598 s vs ~72 s), which is too slow for the guide and the CI notebook timeout. The eager CSR path is a deliberate speedup, not a code smell.
- **Baking `max_dim` into the notebook** changes what readers copy.
- **Excluding the notebook from CI** (as `integrate_dice_solver` already is) loses coverage of this guide.

Whether the ~797 MB CSR copy can be reduced, or matrix-free CPU performance narrowed, is a question for the Fulqrum maintainers and is being pursued separately; this change unblocks CI in the meantime.

`max_dim=300` caps each spin sector, bounding the subspace to ≤ 90k (well under the memory ceiling) while keeping the fast CSR path and a substantial subspace.

<hr>

This PR was generated by Claude Opus 4.8 under my guidance.

pullRequests.title: Loosen the energy tolerance in test_fermion.py
pullRequests.body:
`test_diagonalize_fermionic_hamiltonian_basic` asserted its energy with `places=2` (a tolerance of 0.005 Ha), which is tighter than the spread the method actually has with `samples_per_batch=10` and `max_iterations=5`.

## What I measured

Scanning 200 seeds through `self.rng`, pure Python. Energy error `|result.energy + nuclear_repulsion_energy - exact_energy|`:

| stat | value (Ha) |
|---|---|
| min | 0.0014 |
| median | 0.0078 |
| mean | 0.0085 |
| stdev | 0.0044 |
| p95 | 0.0175 |
| max | 0.0256 |

The `places=2` threshold **fails for 156 of 200 seeds (78%)**. The committed seed gives 0.0036, in the best ~15% of the distribution, so the assertion passed by luck rather than because it described the method's accuracy.

Failure counts: `places=2` → 156/200, `delta=0.02` → 2, `delta=0.025` → 1, `delta=0.03` → 0, `delta=0.05` → 0.

## The change

`assertAlmostEqual(..., places=2)` → `assertAlmostEqual(..., delta=0.05)`, about twice the observed worst case and above mean+6σ. I picked 0.05 over the tighter 0.03 because the tail is still filling in — the max grew from 0.0185 at n=50 to 0.0256 at n=200. `delta=` rather than `places=1` because it states the intended tolerance directly, and `places` cannot express anything between 0.005 and 0.05.

The looser bound still has teeth: the SCF→CASCI correlation window here is ~0.13 Ha, so it fails if SQD recovers less than ~62% of the correlation energy, against ~93% today.

## Measured and left alone

`assertLess(sci_dim, 0.5 * fci_dim)` held for 200/200 seeds, though not by much. With `symmetrize_spin=True` the subspace is square, so `sci_dim` only takes values k²; the largest observed k=39 gives 48.5% of `fci_dim`, and the next reachable value k=40 gives 51%. The margin is one lattice step, but the bound measures something real about this sample-and-iteration budget, so it is left as is.

Worth recording: k=39 is not a ceiling. It is where `max_iterations=5` stops the growth, and k is still climbing when it does (one seed traces 11 → 21 → 32 → 37 → 39 across its five iterations). Raising the iteration count carries k well past it — k=53 at 12 iterations for that seed — with the energy error collapsing to 6e-5 as the subspace approaches the full space. That is SQD converging as intended, and it means the 0.5 bound is a statement about the configured budget, not about the method.

The rest:

- The spin-square checks agree to at most 1.5e-14. They compare the same quantity computed on the SCI vector and on its FCI expansion, so the default `places=7` is effectively an exactness check.
- The energy assertion in the numpy-bitstrings test is exact (diff 0.0) for every seed: H₂/STO-3G has `fci_dim` 4 and the test passes in all four determinants, so the subspace is the full space.
- The `max_dim` assertions hit their caps for every seed; `max_dim` truncates, so they are structural.
- The `seed=12345` reproducibility assertions hold exactly across seeds; both runs use a literal seed.
- `test/test_configuration_recovery.py` has no loose tolerance: its seeded cases use occupancies of exactly 0.0 or 1.0 and assert exact equality.

## On the fixed seed in `setUp()`

Kept, and no per-seed parametrization added. The seed was never the problem; a tolerance narrower than the method's spread was, which made the seed load-bearing. With `delta=0.05` any seed passes, so the committed one is a convenience again. Parametrizing would multiply a PySCF CASCI per seed for information the tolerance already encodes.

No release note: this changes no public API and no library behavior.

<hr>

This pull request was generated by Claude Opus 5 under my guidance.

pullRequests.title: fix symmetrized count aggregation
pullRequests.body: Fixed the ranking of sampled CI strings when ``symmetrize_spin=True`` in `qiskit_addon_sqd.fermion.diagonalize_fermionic_hamiltonian`. If the same string was sampled in both spin sectors, its alpha and beta counts were previously ranked separately rather than being added together. This could cause a lower-weight string to be retained when ``max_dim`` truncated the subspace.
